senses: A young hen, especially one less than a year old.
ety: From Middle English polet, pulet, from Anglo-Norman pullet, Old French poulet (“young chicken”); polette (“young hen”), from poule (“hen”), from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine form of pullus. Doublet of poult. Compare also Middle English pulle. By surface analysis, pull(us) + -et.
examples: They died not because the Pullets would not feed: but because the Devil foresaw their death, he contrived that abstinence in them.

senses: A Korean dish of sliced pork belly that is typically cooked at the table.
A Korean-style restaurant where servings of meat and rice can be requested repeatedly within an allotted time period, with patrons cooking their food at the table.
ety: Borrowed from Korean 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal, literally “three-layered meat”), referring to the layered appearance of the fat.
examples: The best part of eating in a samgyeopsal restaurant is the atmosphere – a rollicking party punctuated by soju shots, pork strips sizzling on a grill and shouts for “one more serving, please!”

senses: Adhering or relating to nominalism.
ety: From nominal + -ist.
examples: Yet even in the basic controversies of that time we can detect something akin to materialism in the nominalist view concerning universals, which reveals a certain interest in physical nature and in concreteness.

senses: a celebration
ety: From Yiddish שׂמחה (simkhe), from Hebrew שִׂמְחָה (simkhá, literally “happiness”).
examples: After the wedding, I received a letter from the bride and her family with profuse thanks for enabling them and the Jewish community of Sheboygan to witness and participate in a "wonderful, traditional simcha"

senses: Mazy, windy, zigzagging in its motion.
ety: From jink + -y.
examples: He's also quite jinky off his feet. He steps through tackles and offloads there are no frills. He brings other players into the game.
Coming out second best then, he then tried a jinky dribble from right to left, only to find McCann standing in his way again.
Unfortunately it was my faster, jinkier pals who could get past the security guards and I'd always end up getting stopped.

senses: An extinct early Eocene mammal (Hyracotherium leporinum), ancestral to the modern horse.
ety: Originally a genus name, Eohippus, formed in New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”). By surface analysis, eo- + Latin hippus.
examples: An eohippus may "evolve" into a horse, but when we say that a society of hunters and gatherers evolves into a farming village, we are using the word "evolves" as a metaphor for a process of directional change.

senses: A ditch or moat.
ety: From Middle English fosse, from Old French fosse, from Latin fossa (“ditch, trench”).
examples: Elberich endeavours to persuade her to become a Christian, and espouse Otnit; and to convince her of the incapacity of her gods, he tumbles their images into the fosse.

senses: Impressively large or luxurious.
Tyrannical or brutally oppressive.
ety: From Latin Pharaōn- (stem of Pharaō (“Pharaoh”)) + -ic, originally modelled on German pharaonisch.
examples: Mark Zuckerberg sculpts his pharaonic Hawaii compound. He and his ilk own the present.

senses: A man's shirt-bosom.
An ornamental front panel on a woman's bodice.
A breastplate.
A film of air trapped by specialized hairs against the body of an aquatic insect, and which acts as an external gill.
ety: Borrowed from French plastron, from Italian piastrone, augmentive of piastra (“breastplate”), from Latin emplastrum (“plaster”), from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron), from ἔμπλαστος (émplastos, “daubed, plastered”), from ἔμπλασσειν (émplassein, “to mould, form”).
examples: The plastron of a diving beetle is not directly a source of oxygen, but acts as a gill, acquiring oxygen from the surrounding water.

senses: The act of dissociating or disuniting; a state of separation; disunion.
A defence mechanism where certain thoughts or mental processes are compartmentalised in order to avoid emotional stress to the conscious mind.
ety: Borrowed from French dissociation, from Latin dissociātiō(n).
examples: Project MONARCH could be best described as a form of structured dissociation and occultic integration, carried out in order to compartmentalize the mind into multiple personalities within a systematic framework.

senses: One who practices criminology.
ety: From criminology + -ist.
examples: I have the strongest suspicion that the whole incident is a ridiculous mare's nest, bred in the fantastic imagination of an enthusiastic criminologist.
Not according to professor James Alan Fox, a criminologist at Northeastern University in Boston who has been studying mass murder for the past three decades.
When he finished his stint in Brooklyn, Weisburd decided to team up with Larry Sherman, another young criminologist.

senses: The act of making plural.
ety: From plural + -ization.
examples: In English pluralization usually involves adding an 'S', but not always.

senses: An upright (or formerly upright) slab containing engraved or painted decorations or inscriptions; a stela.
Any carved or engraved surface.
ety: From Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē, “upright rock; pillar; column”), plural form στῆλαι (stêlai). Doublet of stela.
examples: It appears, that when any one of the family died, a stelè to his memory was added to the tomb.
The Australian stele, or grave-pillar.
Two large hieroglyphed steles incised upon the face of a projecting mass of boldly rounded cliff.

senses: An actor who specializes in tragic roles.
A playwright who writes tragedies.
ety: From Middle English tragedyen, from Old French tragediane (French tragédien), equivalent to tragedy + -ian.
examples: Greene died of a debauch; and Marlowe, the gracer of tragedians, perished in an ignominious brawl.

senses: The spirit or soul.
ety: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “I blow, breathe”). Doublet of neume.
examples: But bound to reach out and beyond this flesh. / Become Pneuma

senses: Not circumcised, intact.
Not Jewish or not Muslim; gentile.
Spiritually impure; irreligious.
ety: From Middle English uncircumcised, equivalent to un- + circumcised. Subsidiary definitions are much influenced by traditions of the Abrahamic religions.
examples: A child who is born to an uncircumcised girl is not allowed to live; as one old woman said, 'only women, not children can have children'
In my tradition, an uncircumcised male cannot be heir to his father's wealth, cannot marry or officiate in tribal rituals.
Surprisingly, few physicians know how to care for uncircumcised boys.

senses: A farewell, a goodbye; especially a fond farewell, or a lasting or permanent farewell.
ety: From Middle English adieu also adew, adewe, adue, from Old French adieu (“to God”), a shortening of a Dieu vous comant (“I commend you to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Doublet of adios.
examples: We bid our final adieus to our family, then boarded the ship, bound for America.
As Noyes bade me adieu and rode off northward in his car I began to walk slowly toward the house.
At the of his so remote, so near, 1884 summer Van, before leaving Ardis, was to make a visit of adieu to Ada's larvarium.

senses: A fluid that has exuded from somewhere; especially one that has exuded from a pore of an animal or plant.
ety: From exude + -ate (noun-forming suffix).
examples: The whitish lines of exudate seem at times to penetrate even between the straight tubes . . .
When this is done, one should leave the poppy for some time, then return to it and gather any further exudate.

senses: slightly painful, akin to being pinched
prone or designed to pinch
ety: From pinch + -y.
examples: I pushed my cropped hair up and away from the back of my neck where it was pinchy and itching.
It's a rare treat in these days when anyone can truck in a case of trendy flavors, set out a few pinchy wire chairs and call the whole sterile spread an ice cream parlor.
I can't keep still. I feel like I'm caught in a trap — my tight corset and pinchy shoes don't help.

senses: A short-horned goat antelope native to mountainous terrain in southern Europe; Rupicapra rupicapra.
The traditional colour of chamois leather.
An absorbent cloth used for cleaning and polishing, formerly made of chamois leather.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French chamois, from Late Latin camox, from Gaulish camox (5th c. AD, Polemius Silvius), probably from an extinct Alpine language (Raetic, Ancient Ligurian), possibly Proto-Indo-European *kem- (“without horns”). Compare also Old High German gamiza (“chamois”) (whence modern German Gämse).
examples: I took them, breathed on them, polished them with a chamois and hung them on the chandelier.
Mirrors can be cleaned with warm water and ammonia or vinegar and polished with a chamois.
Once your paint has been restored, drying your car with a chamois is just about all you have to do to restore the luster.

senses: An eye lesion.
A displeasing sight; something prominently ugly or unsightly.
ety: From Middle English eye sor, eie-sor, eyen soore, eæge-sare, equivalent to eye + sore.
examples: The building, towering over its surroundings with its square concrete frame and reflective walls of gold-tinted glass, was an eyesore visible throughout the city.

senses: A contrail consisting of chemicals or biological agents deliberately sprayed at high altitudes, according to certain conspiracy theories.
ety: Blend of chemical + trail, modelled on contrail, late 1990s.
examples: You and me watching / Chemtrails is where we belong / That's what I mean when we talk in this jetstream

senses: A mixture of cornstarch and water with unusual physical properties.
ety: Named for a sticky substance in Bartholomew and the Oobleck (1949), children's story by Dr. Seuss.
examples: How many people found that the oobleck was different from the flour?
Pour the oobleck into a water table or into plastic tubs to place on tables.
I know from personal experience that it's not fun to be covered with oobleck.

senses: Something or someone that is physically attractive.
Something that is a remarkable example of its type.
ety: Either a back-formation from beauty or a clipping of thereof.
examples: That new car of yours is a real beaut.
In his most famous quip, La Guardia once remarked, “When I make a mistake it's a beaut!”
Both of them were used to long surveillance stints. This looked like it might be a beaut.

senses: A small guitar-like stringed instrument with five courses of eighteen to fifteen strings, originating in traditional Andean folk music.
ety: From Spanish charango, onomatopoeic, or perhaps a corruption of charanga.
examples: One song the group performed on Thursday, “La Partida,” featured lovely bell harmonics from the guitars, a shifting pattern of cross‐rhythms on the guitar‐like charango, and a quena lead.

senses: A hollow, round, Japanese traditional doll modeled after Bodhidharma, the founder of the Zen sect of Buddhism.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 達磨 (daruma), from Sanskrit धर्म (dhárma, “law; morality; code”), used as a clipping of 菩提達磨 (Bodaidaruma, “Bodhidharma”). Doublet of Dharma.
examples: Like a daruma doll, you knock it over and it rights itself.
This combination of piety and fun also accounts for the continued popularity of roly-poly darumas, popular doll-like figures named after Bodhidharma.

senses: To modulate a tone's frequency.
To sing like a bird, especially with trills.
To cause to quaver or vibrate.
To be quavered or modulated; to be uttered melodiously.
ety: Perhaps onomatopoeic.
examples: Her voice more sweet than warbling sound, Tho’ sung by nightingale or lark, Her eyes such lustre dart around, Compar’d to them the sun is dark.
In the swamp in secluded recesses, / A shy and hidden bird is warbling a song.

senses: A day appointed for a meeting intended to amicably resolve a dispute; also the meeting held on such a day.
A day devoted to love.
ety: Inherited from Middle English loveday; equivalent to love + day.
examples: In our period, all the people of England made lovedays, from the richest to the poorest.

senses: A distance from which sound is still audible.
ety: From ear + shot.
examples: I'll row out on the lake but stay within earshot.
Loola glances about her to make sure that nobody is within earshot, then speaks at last almost in a whisper.
When Atticus was out of earshot Jem yelled after him: “I thought I wanted to be a lawyer but I ain’t so sure now!”

senses: The French resistance movement during World War II, or other similar movements elsewhere.
ety: Borrowed from French maquis, from Corsican machja (related to Italian macchia), ultimately from Latin macula. Doublet of macula.
examples: By this time O.S. membership numbered some 4,500, and many of those who escaped imprisonment either fled abroad or formed the nucleus of a growing maquis in the more inaccessible parts of the country.

For many weeks after I finished Bodyguard of Lies, Alan Turing stuck in my mind. He seemed so incongruous a figure to be mixed up with the cut-throat maquis and sinister double-agents who populated the rest of the book.

senses: A character, usually a girl, who has an obsessive and possessive side regarding their crush, ready to use violent (if not murderous) means to maintain an exclusive bond.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese ヤンデレ (yandere), a portmanteau of 病んでる (yanderu), contraction of 病んでいる (yande iru), progressive tense of 病む (yamu, “to be sick”), and デレデレ (dere-dere, “in a lovey-dovey, infatuated, or lovestruck manner”, adverb). Developed on the model of tsundere (“being cold and even hostile towards another person before gradually showing a warm and caring side over time”).
examples: And it finally answered the question as to whether Senjougahara is tsundere or yandere.

senses: A saddle tree maker.
ety: From Middle English fuster, fuystour, fuystor, from Anglo-Norman fuster, Old French fuyster, fust, ultimately from Latin fūstis. Compare French fût, Old French fustier.
examples: There were the Fusters, not to be confused with Fusters who wove fustians ; the Sadler's Fusters made the wooden frame for saddles, which used to be much more elaborate affairs than our modern saddles are.
There were some leather-workers, as 4 or 5 curriers or tanners, 2 kissers, 6 or 7 saddlers or fusters.
It was the task of the fusters, or joiners, to make the wooden saddlebows while the painters were employed to decorate the completed saddles.

senses: A period or occasion of general license, in which the passions or vices have riotous indulgence; a period of unrestrained revelry.
ety: From Saturnalia (“a festival of the winter solstice”).
examples: They lodged men and women on the same floor; and with the night there began a saturnalia of debauchery—scenes such as never before had been witnessed in America.
Yet if he remained, it would simply mean that his own and Hagthorpe's crews would join in the saturnalia and increase the hideousness of events now inevitable.
It was a raw, violent, guzzling saturnalia that spilled obstreperously through the woods to the officers' club and spread up into the hills toward the hospital and the antiaircraft-gun emplacements.

senses: Agitated, confusing.
ety: From fluster + -ing.
examples: To me it seems, Mabel, that whenever a thing is really grand and potent, it has a quiet majesty about it, that is altogether unlike the frothy and flustering manner of smaller matters, and so it was with them rapids.
Although at times my prac experiences were flustering and frustrating, I have gained many new insights into catering for the individual needs of children.
There is nothing more flustering than to wrestle with an unfamiliar piece of equipment in the presence of a class!

senses: A person who stokes, especially one on a steamship or steam train, who stokes coal in the boilers.
A device for stoking a fire; a poker.
A device that feeds coal into a furnace, etc., automatically.
A person who pedals on the back of a tandem bicycle.
ety: From Middle Dutch stoker (“stoker”), from Middle Dutch stoken (“to stoke, incite”, literally “to poke, jab, thrust”), ultimately equivalent to stoke + -er. More at stoke. Compare typologically Russian кочега́р (kočegár) (akin to кочерга́ (kočergá, “poker”)).
examples: He held strongly to the black-ganger's philosophy - what is the use of all the radar and guns and torpedoes if you don't have the engineers and stokers to put them in the right position?
As we reported was to occur, two of Saltley's stoker-fitted 2-10-0s, Nos. 92165/7, have been stripped of their stokers at Crewe works.

senses: To catch in a net; ensnare.
To surround as by a net.
ety: From be- + net.
examples: Being thus benetted round with villains

senses: Any Chinese martial art.
A modern exhibition and full-contact sport based on traditional Chinese martial arts, created in the People's Republic of China. Also known as modern wushu or contemporary wushu.
ety: From Mandarin 武術／武术 (wǔshù, “martial techniques”).
examples: The techniques of contemporary wushu are indeed those which at one time were used for self-defense, but the basis and development of wushu are different from kung fu.

senses: Charcoal; coke.

A pointed stick, which when placed with the point against another piece of wood, and spun rapidly in alternate directions with the aid of attached cords, produces enough heat by friction to create a fire; a fire drill.
A wine glass.
A Middle Eastern falcon, probably the lanner.
ety: A back-formation from charcoal (interpreted as chark coal).
examples: A good chark will sometimes take as many as eight or ten bustards or five or six gazelles in the course of a morning.

senses: Resembling or containing flint; hard like flint.
Showing a lack of emotion.
Having a taste characteristic of certain white wines, especially Chablis, supposed to evoke the sensation of flint striking steel.
ety: From flint + -y.
examples: It was late at night and frosty; high above them on the hills the cloppety clop, cloppety clop of a horse's hooves picking their way on the flinty stone track died away in the distance.
Public opinion has turned flintier in recent years on welfare spending.
While the texture of his playing was often flinty, his licks and leads were flush with feeling.

senses: Like a maniac; insane; frenzied.
ety: From maniac + -al.
examples: He suddenly exploded into about three seconds of maniacal laughter and stopped again.
